Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D deficiency was not associated with a higher risk of post-stroke depression at 3 months.
Sentence: "The incidence of PSD was not significantly different between the two groups at the 3-month (5.8% vs. 4.7%, p = 0.358) and 12-month (11.6% vs. 10.2%, p = 0.364) follow-up."
Measured as: post-stroke depression incidence at 3-month follow-up
Population: Adult patients with first-ever stroke with vitamin D levels available within 3 months before stroke
Intervention: Vitamin D deficiency (25(OH)D < 20 ng/mL), observational exposure
Comparator: Normal vitamin D levels (25(OH)D 30-80 ng/mL)
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 1,516
baseline_vitamin_d_status: mixed

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Among women supplemented with 800 IU vitamin D, those who remained vitamin D deficient before delivery had a significantly higher incidence of depression than those who reached insufficiency.
Sentence: "The incidence of depression in patients in vitamin D deficiency group following vitamin D supplementation was significantly higher than insufficiency group and reached statistical significance (P < 0.001)."
Measured as: incidence of prenatal depression
Population: Pregnant women diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency at 12-14 weeks of gestation, single tertiary hospital in Chengdu, China
Intervention: Vitamin D 800 IU daily from 14 weeks of gestation
Comparator: Women who achieved vitamin D insufficiency after supplementation versus those who remained deficient
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 1,365
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

{
  "rationale": "The studies enrolled clinically distinct populations (patients with first-ever stroke vs vitamin D-deficient pregnant women) and evaluated different exposures (baseline vitamin D status vs achieved status after daily supplementation).",
